blurb: A ground-hugging prairie native that sprawls into a 4-foot mat of finely cut leaves and opens satiny wine-magenta chalices from April until hard frost — one of the longest-blooming xeric plants there is, anchored by a woody taproot that makes it essentially drought-proof.
water: Low; xeric once established — deep taproot needs no supplemental water
spread: Sprawling stems from one deep taproot; widens to 2–5 ft as a single crown; self-sows modestly
seasons: Wine-magenta cups April to hard frost over deeply cut foliage; dies back completely in winter
wildlife: Native bees; larval host and nectar source for the gray hairstreak butterfly
deer: Deer resistant; rabbits will browse the foliage

care.hardiness: Rated USDA zones 4–8 by most authorities and 3–9 by Plant Select, with reports of zone 3 hardiness in well-drained ground — comfortably tough for Boulder's zone 5b–6a. Plant Select grows it to about 6,200 ft on the Front Range. It is a genuine Colorado native rather than an import: its native range across the southern Great Plains takes in Colorado, and CSU Extension lists it among the native herbaceous perennials recommended for Colorado landscapes.[1][2][3][5][6]
care.planting: Set out spring-planted nursery stock after the mid-May last frost, or plant in early fall. Buy it as a young container plant and get it in the ground promptly: the woody taproot can thicken to several inches across and makes established plants very hard to move, so choose the spot once. In a container give it a deep pot and gritty mineral mix — a shallow pot fights the taproot, and the crown rots if the mix stays wet.[1][4]
care.sun: Full sun is where it flowers hardest; Plant Select allows full to part sun. It takes hot south- and west-facing exposures that cook other perennials, which is exactly the niche it fills on a Front Range hell strip.[2][4]
care.soil: Easily grown in dry to medium, well-drained soil, and genuinely adaptable — it tolerates clay, loam, sand and shallow rocky ground, and does fine in infertile soil. Sharp drainage matters far more than fertility, and it is at home in our neutral-to-alkaline soils.[1][2][3]
care.water: Low. The long woody taproot — up to about 5 in thick — is what makes it drought-tolerant, so once established it needs no supplemental water. Plant Select notes that giving it *less* water keeps it more compact instead of sprawling as wide, and NC State warns it especially wants good drainage in wet winter conditions.[3][4][2]
care.spacing: Space 18–24 in apart and let the stems knit together; a single plant fills 2–5 ft across, so a few plants cover a lot of ground.[2][1]
care.propagation: Seed is the practical route — it is the strategy NC State recommends, and the plant self-sows readily where it is happy. Division and transplanting are not realistic once the taproot is established, so treat mature clumps as permanent.[3][1][4]
care.sow: Scarify the hard seed coat first — rubbing it on coarse sandpaper markedly improves germination — then sow outdoors about 1/8 in deep in late summer or fall so it gets natural winter chilling.[4]
care.bloom: The long season is the whole point: Plant Select gives April to hard frost, NC State late spring through summer into early fall, and MBG a May–June peak. Each 1.5–2.5 in magenta chalice has a white spot at the base of its five petals, opens in the morning and closes at evening, then closes permanently once pollinated.[2][3][1][4]
care.maintenance: Very low. Cut the whole plant back to the base each spring — it dies back completely in winter and re-emerges from the crown. Pinching the stems back keeps it tighter if it is crowding neighbours, and Plant Select notes it is long-lived and well-behaved, needing almost nothing after 5–10 years. Expect some dieback in late summer after the heaviest flowering.[2][4][3]
care.selfsow: It self-sows where conditions suit it, though not aggressively. Plant Select's advice is the practical one: pull unwanted seedlings while they are young, before the taproot gets a hold and makes them hard to remove.[2][3]
care.troubles: No serious insect or disease problems. Crown rot is the real risk and it comes from poorly drained soil, not from cold — the failure mode here is a wet, heavy spot, not a cold winter. Rabbits will chew the foliage.[1][4]

edible.summary: No documented culinary use in the horticultural authorities; grown purely as a xeric ornamental groundcover.[1][3]
edible.caution: None of the authorities consulted document a food use for purple poppy mallow, so this guide treats it as inedible — don't eat it. No part is recorded as notably poisonous either, and NC State lists no toxicity concern, but absence of a poisoning record is not evidence of edibility. The plant's own defence is chemical-free anyway: what protects it is a taproot too deep to dig and foliage deer leave alone.[1][3]
